arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: General Clement argued the FCC must allocate spectrum for the public interest. He stated auctions assign spectrum to the most effective users.
Mr. Franklin argued the Bankruptcy Code permits overriding FCC determinations. He claimed this allows bankrupt companies to retain specific assets.
Mr. Verrilli argued the FCC revoked licenses solely due to deferred payments. He stated this action occurred while NextWave reorganized in bankruptcy.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The dispute centers on whether federal bankruptcy law supersedes FCC regulatory authority. The FCC asserts its power to revoke licenses based on public interest. NextWave argues bankruptcy protections shield its assets during reorganization.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The FCC wants the Court to uphold its license revocation. It seeks to prevent bankruptcy courts from overriding public interest decisions.
NextWave wants the Court to protect its bankruptcy reorganization. It seeks to keep its spectrum licenses during the process.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The FCC argues Congress directed it to allocate spectrum for the public interest. It claims bankruptcy judges cannot override this regulatory determination.
NextWave argues the Bankruptcy Code permits it to defer payments. It claims this protection allows it to retain licenses during reorganization.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between bankruptcy law and federal regulation. It determines whether agencies can enforce public interest standards against bankrupt entities. The outcome shapes how spectrum licenses are protected during financial distress.
